cards.front: Cellular respiration is the process in which cells break down {{c1::sugar (glucose)}} with oxygen and release energy.
cards.quote: Cellular respiration is the process in which cells break down sugar (glucose) with oxygen and release energy.
cards.section: Go further: the pathway inside cells

cards.front: Almost all plant, animal and fungus cells have which organelle, where most cellular respiration happens?
cards.back: The mitochondrion (plural: mitochondria).
cards.quote: Almost all plant, animal, and fungus cells have mitochondria, with a few exceptions.
cards.section: Go further: the pathway inside cells

cards.front: Write the word equation for cellular respiration.
cards.back: Sugar (glucose) + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
cards.quote: sugar (glucose) + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy Plants make glucose by photosynthesis.
cards.section: Go further: the pathway inside cells

cards.front: How are breathing and cellular respiration different, and how do they connect?
cards.back: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration happens inside cells. Breathing brings in the oxygen respiration uses and carries out the carbon dioxide it gives off.
cards.quote: Breathing is not cellular respiration; the table shows how they connect.
cards.section: Go further: the pathway inside cells

cards.front: Besides glucose, what other food molecules can cells release energy from?
cards.back: Fats and proteins, such as those in a peanut.
cards.quote: Cells can also release energy from fats and proteins, such as those in a peanut.
cards.section: Go further: the pathway inside cells

cards.front: A student says, "Plants make their own food, so their cells do not need cellular respiration." Is that correct?
cards.back: No. Plant cells almost always have mitochondria and also break down sugar with oxygen to release energy.
cards.quote: Almost all plant, animal, and fungus cells have mitochondria, with a few exceptions.
cards.section: Go further: the pathway inside cells

cards.front: Name one kind of cell that has no mitochondria.
cards.back: A mature red blood cell in mammals.
cards.quote: A few cells do not have mitochondria, such as mature red blood cells in mammals.
cards.section: Cells without mitochondria

cards.front: Where does the energy released by respiration go?
cards.back: Some powers cell work, such as muscle contraction. Some always leaves as thermal energy.
cards.quote: The released energy powers cell work, and some always leaves as thermal energy.

cards.front: Thermal energy is the energy of {{c1::moving particles}}.
cards.quote: Some of it leaves as thermal energy, the energy of moving particles.
cards.section: Follow the released energy

cards.front: Why can your body stay near 37 °C on a cold day?
cards.back: Your body loses thermal energy to cooler air, but respiration keeps releasing more. Staying warm depends on balancing heat made with heat lost.
cards.quote: Your body usually loses thermal energy to cooler air, while respiration keeps releasing more.
cards.section: Follow the released energy

cards.front: Does food turn into energy when cells respire? What happens to energy?
cards.back: No. Food does not turn into energy, and energy is never used up. It only changes form.
cards.quote: Food does not turn into energy, and energy is never used up; it only changes form.
cards.section: Follow the released energy

cards.front: In a flask model of sprouting seeds, you warm the water bath from 10 °C to 25 °C. What happens to the rate of respiration and the balloon?
cards.back: In the model, within its suitable temperature range, the rate rises and the balloon gets more carbon dioxide. Warming helps only within a suitable range.
cards.quote: Warming helps only within a suitable range.

cards.front: A flask of sprouting seeds is sealed so no fresh air enters. What happens to respiration with oxygen after a while?
cards.back: It slows, because the oxygen runs low and this kind of respiration needs oxygen.
cards.quote: Oxygen matters to respiration that uses oxygen.

cards.front: An open flask holds 5 sprouting seeds. You use 10 seeds instead. How fast does the balloon fill, compared with before?
cards.back: About twice as fast in this model: more living cells respiring give off more carbon dioxide in total.
cards.quote: more living cells respiring give off more carbon dioxide in total
cards.section: Explore: test a flask of living cells

cards.front: Does adding more and more sugar keep speeding up respiration?
cards.back: No. Added sugar helps only to a point.
cards.quote: Added sugar helps only to a point.

cards.front: {{c1::Fermentation}} is a way to break down sugar without oxygen.
cards.quote: Fermentation is a way to break down sugar without oxygen.
cards.section: Read the evidence the second film did not show

cards.front: Why is oxygen used a better measure than carbon dioxide given off when testing baker's yeast?
cards.back: Yeast ferments even when air is present, and fermentation also gives off carbon dioxide. Oxygen used measures only respiration with oxygen.
cards.quote: Because yeast ferments even in air, as the second film showed, oxygen used is the better measure for yeast.
cards.section: Read the evidence the second film did not show

cards.front: Fresh peas give off 30 to 46 mg of carbon dioxide per kg per hour at 0 °C and 220 to 322 at 20 °C. Compare the lowest 20 °C value with the highest 0 °C value. About how many times larger is it?
cards.back: 220 ÷ 46 is about 4.8 times. Even the lowest value at 20 °C is above the highest at 0 °C, so the peas respire faster at 20 °C.
cards.quote: Far-apart rows do not: the lowest value at 20 °C, 220, is above the highest at 0 °C, 46.
cards.section: Read the evidence the second film did not show

cards.front: A yeast strain at 30 °C used 2.7 mmol of oxygen per gram of dry yeast per hour in 20.9% oxygen and 1.7 in 1.0% oxygen. About how many times as much oxygen did it use in 20.9%?
cards.back: 2.7 ÷ 1.7 is about 1.6 times. Oxygen used fell as the oxygen supply went down.
cards.quote: Even so, oxygen used counts only the respiration that uses oxygen.
cards.section: Read the evidence the second film did not show

cards.front: The pea table lists carbon dioxide given off from 0 to 25 °C. What can it not tell you?
cards.back: What too much heat does to respiration, because the table stops at 25 °C.
cards.quote: The table stops at 25 °C, so it cannot show what too much heat does.
cards.section: Read the evidence the second film did not show

cards.front: Two thermoses hold equal masses of peas: one living and sprouting, one boiled and cooled to room temperature. Only the living thermos warms above the room. What does this show, and why is the boiled thermos needed?
cards.back: The warmth comes from the living peas' respiration. The boiled peas are the control: dead cells do not respire, so they should not warm.
cards.quote: if only the living peas get warmer than the room, that is good evidence the warmth comes from their respiration.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the pea thermos test, the boiled control also warms above the room. What could be the cause, and what should you do?
cards.back: Microbes on the peas can also release thermal energy. Repeat the test with fresh, clean peas.
cards.quote: Microbes on the peas can also release thermal energy, so a warm control would mean the test needs fresh, clean peas.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Yeast stirred into warm sugar water foams and fills a balloon. Would it fill faster or more slowly in ice-cold water, and why?
cards.back: Probably more slowly: cells in cold water should work more slowly, so less carbon dioxide is given off.
cards.quote: In ice-cold water they should work more slowly.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Sealed yeast in sugar water has used up its oxygen, yet its balloon keeps filling. Using the lesson's ideas, what explains this?
cards.back: Yeast can ferment, breaking down sugar without oxygen and giving off carbon dioxide. Respiration with oxygen slows when oxygen runs low, but fermentation does not need it.
cards.quote: The model leaves out fermentation, so real yeast in a sealed bottle can keep filling a balloon.
cards.section: Explore: test a flask of living cells

cards.front: Does a lot of sugar make yeast respire with oxygen more or less?
cards.back: Less. A lot of sugar makes yeast ferment more and respire with oxygen less.
cards.quote: A lot of sugar makes yeast ferment more and respire with oxygen less.
cards.section: Yeast can use fermentation
